Heidegger tacitly expresses his growing disenchantment with a Fuhrer turning from statesmanlike to coercive ways to persuade his following, and a total state bent on coercively politicizing all walks of life, allowing no room for the independent counsel of his educated coterie of guardians, by way of a reduction, begun in 1935, of the polis to a prepolitical originarity that is the source of not only the political but also the philosophical, poetic, religious, and other creative human endeavors. In the context of the tragic phronesis of the conflict between family piety and royal ediction in Sophocles' Antigone, Heidegger finds that polis is not merely a geographically located state (Staat) or city (Stadt) but, more basically, a historical site (Stiitte) virtually identical to the ontological site of Da-sein in which a unique humankind (for example, Greek being-here, German being-there) "takes place" (statt-Jindet, statt-hat), is "granted stead" (gestattet, upermitted"), and in this "leeway" (Spielraum) of allotted time and historical place makes its unique "homestead" (Heimstatt) befitting its historical

Theodore Kisiel

destiny. This historical site of Da-sein is the "pole" of the polis, from which human beings receive their stance and status in the state and ac-

quire their stature in each of their historical instantiations. This " 'politics' in the supreme and authentic sense" thus takes place at the supreme site of radical historical transition displayed by the Greek tragedy, which glosses the ox·ymoronic status of the tragic heroine (Antigone) as hypsipolis apolis, at once far beyond and without home and site, unhomely, lonesome, uncanny, singled out for lofty greatness by creating a new home for her people, as well as for the precipitous destruction which was also the fate of Heidegger's more contemporary heroes: Holderlin, Nietzsche, van Gogh, and Schlageter. Around this core of history, Da-sein as polis, not only statesmen and thinkers, but also poets and prophets are gathered together in unity and lonely, untimely, tragic, and contentious dialogue. Politicians (or better, statesmen) are not the only creators of the polis and so the political. Especially in the "land of poets and thinkers," Holderlin's "fatherland," politics finds its origins in poetizing and thinking: "It is from these two prior activities that the Dasein of a people is made fully effective as a people through the state--politics."12

It is from this archaic vantage of Da-sein that Heidegger now criticizes the Nazi claim of the totalitarian character of the political: "These

[Nazi] enthusiasts are now suddenly discovering the 'political' everywhere . .. . But the polis cannot be defined 'politically.' The polis, and precisely it, is therefore not a 'political' concept .... Perhaps the name polis is precisely the word for that realm that constantly became questionable anew, remained worthy of question, and necessitated certain decisions whose truth on each occasion displaced the Greeks into the groundless or the inaccessible."13 Aristotle saw clearly that man was a political animal because he was the animal possessed by speech. But he did not see the full uncanniness that membership in the polis brings, far outstripping the rhetorical as well as the political of a people's state. Holderlin's poetic words, "Since we are a conversation / and can hear from one another," refer to the thoughtful dialogue among solitary creators (poets, thinkers, statesmen) at the very abysses of being. Language here is the original institution of being in the violent words of poetic origin and not just a means of communication for the sake of quick and easy agreement, rhetoric. The community of creators is a combative community of struggle over the extreme issues of being. Hearing from one another, listening to one another, reciprocally involves radically placing each other in question over the radical issues at stake. Rapprochement here is contention, contestation, war, pole-mos. Coming to an understanding is combat: "Conversation here is not communication, but the fundamental happening of radical exposure in the thick of beings." 1 ◄

While chora can mean "land" or "city," when used in the context of the polis it more often means the surrounding countryside; thus, a polis actually consists of a town (asty) and territory (chora) (McEwen 155n4; see also Sallis 116). Looking at the archaeological work ofFrant,ois de Polignac, McEwen describes the placement of sanctuaries in early Greek cities as falling into three areas, with some placed within the inhabited urban area; others established at short distances from the urban area (suburban): and still others located at the limits of the city's territory (chora), some six to twelve kilometers away from the center. McEwen argues that here we see Uthe notion of apolis allowed to appear as a surface woven by the activity of its inhabitants" in "ritual processions from center to urban limit to territorial limit and back again~ (81). The movements from city center to outlands and back constitute the weaving of the city whereby what is constructed

emerges directly from the situated activity of the inhabitants, much like the dance "weaves" the dance floor.

Of particular relevance is the affinity that shows up here between architectural and discursive construction. Both require some sense of place for instantiation to occur, but instantiation itselfresults from spatial dynamics. If in its more archaic sense the chora was a territory made to appear through what McEwen characterizes as a "continual remaking or reweaving of its encompassing surface" (82), an instability becomes apparent in the notion of the polis. It is always bumping up against a limit or boundary that it must exceed while retaining a dependency it wants to overcome. The movements beyond the city's boundaries mark the weaving of the city because the polis cannot thrive without them. In this regard, McEwen remarks that Plato's Republic and Laws are striking in their claim that political order can be thought without this sense of making or weaving integral to the polis (98). From this perspective, the Republic is stillborn, even ifit stems from an engagement with Athens itself, because it utilizes ideas that remain theoretical, since they lack a place from which they can thrive. However, as the Timaeus makes clear, similar misgivings must also have gripped Plato insofar as he attempts to move from the Republic's static ideals-a theory of the perfect city-to a spatial dynamic for those ideals that can move from dialogic discussion to mythical surrogate (Atlantis) to actualization as Athens itself. Crucially, for Plato, the ch6ra takes on far greater import as well, even if at base it is a means to explain how the (eternal, perfect) Forms become individuated beings. There are political ramifications, for instance. A ch6ra is not just the outlying territory on which the city depends. Rather, it becomes a fundamental cosmological principle, the receptacle (hypodochen), the matrix (or womb, metra), for all that comes to be. The import granted the city reminds us that the social is never forgotten in the question of the material. They go together. For things to be what they are, for formal ideals to actualize themselves in experience, they must be illuminated by everyday being. The generative and orchestrating background that gives place remains in its giving.

The Timaeus thereby stages for us a new kind of beginning, one that moves from the realm of the idea to the world of generation, or from static being to vital becoming. This is what Socrates and his comrades desire to generate. and the purpose of the Timaeus is to bring the ideal polis to life as an actual city, one that has a place. Eventually this place will come to correspond with Athens. In making this comparison between Athens and the ideal city, the Timaeus implicitly argues that a beginning is tied to place and memory and that both beginnings and place are woven through the polis. Further, the choric city will be one that not only has a place but encompasses eros. The limits to fabrication can be exceeded through productive eros, an idea that adds to the implicit importance of place a bodily dimension (as well as a reinscription of a maternal feminine within masculinist production, a point Kristeva underscores). In other words, the choric city is where invention comes to life precisely because the chora reworks the distinction between techne andphysis that Plato seems to assume ash is starting point. The chora thus provides Plato a means to explain the movement from Idea to becoming as a form of vital, robust actuality. This relation parallels the connection McEwen sees between dancing and having a place to dance: to give something a place means to see it in action and vice versa. Put differently, human activity is already enworlded. This helps explain the import of the legend about ancient Athens facing off against the Atlante ans. While the Athens of Plato's day appears less noble in comparison, the Athens of old nevertheless comes to embody not just the ideal polis discussed in the Republic but also those ideals further ennobled in agonistic activity.

Despite these insights and explanations, something about the ch6ra remains elusive. resisting determination (see Sallis 3-6). This problem is already noted in the Timaeus. Timaeus tells us that the ch6ra is "most dif-

ficult to catch" and apprehensible only by means of a "bastard reasoning" (51a-b, 52b). The chora is of a third kind that is not really a "kind"; it is a receptacle (hypodoche), which Edward Casey describes as something "at once locatory and yet not itselflocated, permanent and yet invisible, underlying and yet insubstantial" (37). The chora is the matrix of all becoming, yet it declines to be determined, and in this sense, it is not strictly speaking a Form. As Casey argues, then, while ch6ra is not a thing, "it is a locatory matrix/or things" (34), It is what is necessary for the genesis of things, that in which (en ho) and from which (ex hou) they show up and pass away; but the ch6ra also recedes, declining to leave its imprint on things just as it declines to take on the qualities of the things it receives (Timaeus soc). There is a dichotomy between what occurs in the passage to actuality by means of which things show up and their actual showing up. A beginning, even as something unstable or retroactively posited, is never equivalent to what has emerged.

Plato thus deploys the ch6ra to open a theme to which I will return throughout this book, that ambience can never be understood simply as presence. Place is not simply an immediate environment; it includes the background by means of which things show up as what they are. Our everyday environment coheres, but it is choreographed in advance, as it were, so that its particularity is hollowed out beforehand. Such a background recedes, or withdraws, even as it generates. In this sense placing occurs through displacing, a point Derrida makes by showing how the ch6ra disrupts representation itself (and hence rhetoric, too, if it is conceived in terms of symbolicity) even while it remains fundamental for the passage to representation.

Though the Timaeus sometimes waxes large with cosmological import, the older sense of ch6ra as "city" or "land" remains present. The dialogue's attempt to wrestle with the limitations of fabrication (or techne) following the discussion of the ideal city invites us to consider the relation of the chora to the polis and of the polis to its exterior or what lies outside its boundaries. Recall that the region surrounding and sustaining a polis is also called ch6ra. Thus, as was mentioned with respect to McEwen, the chora has a specifically political dimension, being both the boundary of the city and what lies beyond the boundar y. What must be underscored here is the necessity for the polis to go beyond its boundaries to thrive (a reinforcement ofTimaeus's anagke at 47e). Thrownness is neither a 'fact that is finished' nor a Fact that is settled.1 Dasein's facticity is such that as long as it is what it is, Dasein remains in the throw, and is sucked into the turbulence of the "they's" inauthenticity. Thrownness, in which facticity lets itself be seen phenomenally, belongs to Dasein, for which, in its Being, that very Being is an issue. Dasein exists factically. Can Dasein be conceived as an entity for which, in its Being, its potentiality-for-Being is an issue, if this entity, in its very everydayness, has lost itself, and, in falling, 'lives' away from itself? But falling into the world would be phenomenal 'evidence' against the existentiality of Dasein only if Dasein were regarded as an isolated "I" or subject, as a self-point from which it moves away. In that case, the world would be an Object. Falling into the world would then have to be re-Interpreted ontologically as Being-present-at-hand in the manner of an entity within-the-world. Falling reveals an essential ontological structure of Dasein itself. Far from determining its nocturnal side, it constitutes all Dasein's days in their everydayness. It follows that our existential-ontological Interpretation makes no ontical assertion about the 'corruption ofhuman Nature', not because the necessary evidence is lacking, but because the problematic of this Interx8o pretation is prior to any assertion about corruption or incorruption. Falling is conceived ontologically as a kind of motion. But in so far as any faith or

The Being of that disclosed­ ness is constituted by states-of-mind, understanding, and discourse. Its everyday kind of Being is characterized by idle talk, curiosity, and ambiguity. These show us the movement of falling, with temptation, tranquillizing, alienation, and entanglement as its essential characteristics. Because the Timaeus deals pervasively with the question of beginnings, it is appropriate to see it also as a recommencement of the task that was central to the Republic, which is to bring Athens back to its ideal form (at the time of the dialogue, apparently, the interlocutors saw it as less than it had been). What we learn from the Republic is that while the ideal city they describe evokes powerful feelings and approval, it remains an ideal. It misses actuality, and the discussants hope this condition is rectifiable, that this city ideal can be brought to life and seen vigorously exercising as states do (Timaeus 18b). As it is, the ideal city is a dead city. Sallis remarks that, strictly speaking, it is a "technical city," a city of the head achieved through philosophical technique (20). Not only is it a fabricated artifact of thought, but it lacks eros, which is to say, it lacks becoming in a generative sense. The fact that the Republic focuses strongly on controlling eros and all that goes with it, such as "procreation, mating, birth, sexual difference, [and] corporeity itself in its singularity," takes on greater significance in this context (Sallis 26). There is thus a tension between control as something intellectual and life as something that exceeds the intellectual. For this reason, among others, Sallis tells us that from the very beginning, the Timaeus comments on the limits of fabrication, whether as techne or poiesis, with respect to eros (26). This is very much a problem of invention in the sense of finding ways to actualize or enact what are initially only ideas, feelings, or intuitions. That is, the Platonic chora addresses the question of the available means of creation and how we give life to and make a place for (static) ideas. Furthermore, the discussion implicitly evokes a distinction

between the made and the born, or between techni and physis. The chora gains even greater import when we see that it emerges precisely to dissolve such distinctions and give life to artifice.

Friedrich Solmsen argues that we can understand Plato to be wrestling with a problem that reaches far back into debates carried on by the pre-Socratics. How is one to understand genesis, or becoming? Parmenides is held to have dismissed any outright genesis; Empedocles refined Parmenides's thought, suggesting instead that something akin t omixture, achieved through the interactions of the four elements or roots (see chapter 7), could replace genesis. The Timaeus itself addresses this issue, but it does so as a reopening of the question of becoming. Throughout the dialogue, the uncertainty of knowing anything about genesis is remarked, and even the accounts given are characterized as only probable or likely (Timaeus 28b, 44d, 48c-d, 55d, 59c. 66d). ln this regard, the ch6ra can be taken as Plato's attempt to reintroduce the notion of becoming, even ifhe steps back from the more assertive positions of his predecessors (Solmsen 40). At the risk of oversimplifying, we might say that Plato posited this refined notion of genesis as an aid in thinking through how, as Algra puts it, the sensible world participates in the intelligible world (3). Ann Ashbaugh makes a similar point when she claims that the Timaeus was the mast important Platonic dialogue in antiquity because it addressed a fundamental question, one that we have yet to answer definitively: not "what an objective cosmos is, but how it comes to be known by the souln (1). Apropos ofSallis's comment on the limits of fabrication, the Republic already carries in germinal form this very question: haw does one move from ideas, or the realm of the Forms. to the sensible, active world?

This sensible, active world is not one of simple presence or mundane materiality. The Greeks, like other ancient peoples, had a strong sense of what remains hidden, obscure, and withdrawn in the world. Indeed. the ancient sense of the divine was itself tethered to place, as E. V. Walter argues throughout his book Placeways. Thus, we can see Plato's tum to myth (which pervades his dialogues), his evocation of a"bastard reasoning," as bringing together his desire for rationality with his more obscure leanings toward doctrines espoused by initiates of divine mysteries, such as thos e of the Pythagorean and Orphic traditions (see Kingsley).
